overview: This three-page Department of State list of papers indexes correspondence and reports concerning the manufacture, production, and use of artificial wool, also called staple fiber, in Japan from 1934 through early 1936. It traces Joseph D. Holmes’s requests for information, inquiries sent to American consular posts, reports from Kobe and Tokyo, the collection and distribution of fiber, yarn, and cloth samples, and interest from the Departments of Agriculture and Commerce. Later entries concern publicity given to a Tokyo report in the Daily News Record and unsuccessful requests for publicly distributable copies. The underlying correspondence and reports are described in the index but are not reproduced in the supplied pages.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Manufacture of Artificial Wool in Japan
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, compiler unidentified
subfiles.about: A chronological index summarizes correspondence, consular reports, sample transfers, and publication inquiries concerning Japanese artificial wool and staple fiber.
subfiles.summary: The index begins with Joseph D. Holmes’s January 1934 request for information and records instructions to the American consular posts at Tokyo, Kobe, and Nagoya. It notes reports from Tokyo on staple-fiber production and use, together with samples of fiber, yarn, and woven cloth that were circulated among Holmes and the Departments of Agriculture and Commerce. The later entries document a Daily News Record article apparently derived from the consular reporting and requests by H. S. Davis and William Hies for copies of the report. The Department replied that no copies were available for public distribution and referred the final request to the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce.

interest: The index provides a compact reconstruction of how the State Department gathered and circulated industrial intelligence about an emerging Japanese synthetic-textile industry. Of particular value is its record of physical samples—fiber, yarn, and woven cloth—moving among consular officers, federal departments, and an outside requester. The entries concerning the Daily News Record also reveal official concern about how information from a nonpublic consular report reached the trade press. Because only the index is present here, it is especially useful as a guide to the contents and chronology of the larger original file.
